ary** ###### **1.1 Introduction** In the previous edition of our Quarterly Copper Forecast we thought that the uninspiring fundamentals in the first half of 2010 would prevent a new rally from getting underway and cause considerable volatility, with possible ventures down to $6,000/tonne. Although the year did start with a rally to a peak of $7,760/tonne on 7th January, the move was not sustained and prices underwent a sharp correction to a low of a little over $6,200/tonne by 5th February. Once again the market surprised to the upside and at these levels strong buying from bargain hunting investors and consumers alike provided fuel for a recovery and indeed a rally to a new peak above $8,000/tonne in early April, before copper consolidated in the upper $7,000s. Looking at the drivers of these moves and starting with the late January/early February sell-off, this was largely a reflection of the rise in risk aversion the Greek sovereign debt crisis fuelled as well as the positive impact the events had on the US dollar. Compounding these, concerns over a potential tightening of Chinese monetary policy had an additional negative impact on investor sentiment towards copper and in fact the wider commodities sector. Finally, the existence of a substantial speculative long position in copper early in the year made the price of the metal particularly prone to liquidations. More instructive than the fact there was a significant correction in the first quarter was in our view its limited extent as well as its brief duration. Specifically, although we acknowledge that the retracement prices suffered was the most noteworthy since the recent rally began last March, we note that investors and consumers alike saw prices in the $6,200s - well above marginal production costs - as a strong buy signal. Considering the former, strong buying was seen both by speculators who liquidated when copper stood above $7,500/tonne as well as bargain-hunters who had perhaps missed the previous rise. As far as consumers are concerned, we note that last year many had been reluctant to add to their stocks, in part of course due to the exceptionally adverse conditions that weighed on the relevant end-use markets but also as there was an underlying expectation of a correction, given a market in surplus. As a much awaited noteworthy correction never emerged, consumers saw prices “move away” from them over the second half of last year. As a result, the first meaningful correction earlier this year saw consumers aggressively move in, providing essential support for prices. It is worth noting here that the relatively high bottom of the market (cer

tainly in relation to production costs) and strong subsequent recovery in February-April were far from exclusive to copper. For instance, looking at the other five main LME metals’ prices, their February trough was no more than 23% down from their end2009 levels (compared to 15% for copper). Moreover, the recovery that followed, during which copper prices peaked 27% above the aforementioned trough, saw prices of all the other five metals rise by at least 23%, with the star performer, nickel, peaking 62% above its February low recently, as a result of rising stainless steel production. Elsewhere, other commodity markets moved in a similar trajectory over the first four months of the year. As we explain in the relevant section of this chapter, the positive correlation that continued to be in place between copper and other commodity prices is in large part linked to the importance of investment activity in the market currently. The rebound in February-April was also boosted by a rise of Chinese imports, which were fuelled by the emergence of a notable Shanghai-LME premium. **3** Independent - Informed - International 3-Year Copper Forecast - April 2010 **CONFIDENTIAL** LME Stocks as Weeks of Consumption

As such, as we discuss in more detail further on, our projections see surpluses for both the second and third quarters, albeit ones of limited magnitude. A return to deficit is only expected to materialise in the final quarter of the year and even then demand is expected to exceed supply only by a limited amount, leaving the full-year in surplus. The relatively muted recovery in copper’s fundamental conditions in the second and third quarter are key to our projections of a period of consolidation during this time. As we discuss in the investment section later in this chapter, changing attitudes from many commodity investors towards copper and the rather significant long overhang in the market are also expected to prevent the red metal from rallying further from current levels, at least on a sustainable basis. Further gains, with prices establishing themselves comfortably above $8,000/tonne, are only expected to materialise in the last quarter of the year, as the market once again returns to deficit. Coupled with the restocking mentioned earlier, this can also explain the decline in LME inventories. Looking at copper’s immediate fundamentals in more detail, these remain lacklustre in late April. Although as we noted above, LME inventories have been declining in recent weeks, this has largely been due to material shifting to unreported stockpiles (be that consumer stocks or harder to track inventories in China) and the market has, to our understanding, remained in

surplus. Although consumption continues to recover, to-date the rate of this recovery continues to be limited and has merely narrowed the gap between demand and supply. Our quarterly supply-demand analysis shows that over the first three months of the year consumption fell 29,000 tonnes short of output. Although this represents a huge improvement on a year-on-year but also quarter-on-quarter basis, real tightness has yet to emerge in the copper market. As far as the medium to longer term outlook for copper is concerned, GFMS remain positive towards the metal, as we expectations production growth to fall short of increases in consumption. Regarding the latter, demand is expected to grow strongly in all three years of the forecast period, following two years of declines and, by implication, a relatively low base last year. Against this backdrop, the structural constraints to production growth are expected to prevent supply from “catching up” with demand (the former is expected to grow by a compounded 12.6% over the forecast period, while the latter by 18.7%), culminating in what we would describe as a structural deficit in the market. At the same time, as we discuss in the relevant section later in this chapter, the current high level of involvement of investors in the market is expected to continue through to at least the end of 2012. Prices will remain prone to investor liquidations and, given the gap between marginal costs of production and their levels, corrections are likely to be significant. As such, although we forecast prices will reach the mid-$9,000s in 2012, we have maintained lows in the upper $6,000s during that year. ###### **1.2 Economic Assumptions** GFMS’ view on how the global macroeconomic backdrop will develop over the forecast period holds pa

ramount importance for our projections for copper supply, demand and prices. Given the on-going uncertainty in the economic and financial markets, GFMS highlight our economic assumptions in three different, probability weighted scenarios. At the time of writing, the majority of relevant economic indicators continue to paint a largely positive picture for copper demand, even though to-date a noteworthy recovery in consumption has yet to commence in most key markets outside China. As discussed later in this section and in detail in Chapter 3, we expect that this points to an acceleration in consumption growth going forward, at least under our Base Case, which represents the scenario we believe is most likely to materialise. It is worth presenting the key assumptions of our three scenarios, which are discussed in detail in Chapter 2: **Base Case Scenario:** (with a 50% probability outcome). We have revised upwards the majority of our 2010 GDP growth projections under this scenario since the previous edition of the 3-Year Copper Forecast in response to better than expected results over the last few months. The recovery that has already commenced is still expected to gather momentum in 2010, helped by re-stocking, and we expect global GDP to increase by 2.9% in real terms over the year. On a regional basis, acceleration in a number of developing Asian economies coupled with growth in mature markets turning positive contribute to the global figure. In contrast, our projections for growth in 2011 has been scaled down compared to our previous copper quarterly. As European countries and the United States begin address their fiscal imbalances and China and India attempt to keep inflation under control, we would expect the year to see a slow-down in global growth to 2.4%. A marginal acceleration is then forecast for 2012, as consumer spending and other more traditional sources of growth recover. **Scenario B:** (with a 25% probability outcome). A more robust recovery followed by stronger growth is the principal assumption of our most bullish scenario. As real GDP growth in the United States breaches the 3% mark in 2010 and China’s economy expands by nearly 11%, global GDP growth is seen rising by 3.7% over the year, accelerating to 3.8% in 2011 and keeping to a healthy 3.3% in the last year of the period. The higher growth is expected to come at the expense of strong inflation, particularly in the US, where consumer price inflation peaks at 7.5% in 2011. LME Stocks vs Monthly Average Price

Under our most pessimistic scenario, the current buoyancy in the markets proves unjustified, and the recovery proves anaemic, particularly when the private sector takes on the reins. Eventually, as mature economies begin to face their fiscal imbalances and China focuses in keeping its economy from overheating, we would not be surprised if global growth moved into negative territory once again, if only for one or two quarters. As such, growth this year and in 2011 under Scenario C is forecast at 2.1% and 1.7% respectively, with the acceleration in the final year of the forecast period still generating a 2.4% figure, well below the 2000-2008 average. It is worth noting that under this scenario, inflation keeps to extremely low levels throughout 2010-2012, after being in negative territory last year overall. ###### **1.3 The Dollar** Reversing its trend over much of last year, the US dollar has been strengthening against the euro since December 2009. Initially this was a reflection of rising risk aversion, in the aftermath of the Dubai crisis, whereas during much of this year, the Greek sovereign debt crisis has been the key driver of this. Seemingly positive outcomes for a number of US-specific economic indicators have further helped the greenback, as has speculative activity, with information collected through field research confirming notable shorting of the euro having taken place this year. Although we have seen strong support for the dollar:euro rate develop at around 1.33 on numerous occasions in the last few weeks, we would not be surprised if a visit, albeit shortlived, to or even below the 1.30 were to materialise over the next couple months. Although a sustainable return to dollar:euro rates above 1.50 is hard to envisage from current levels, GFMS believe that the low 1.30s are unsustainable and that the euro will recover against the greenback later this year. In large part this is due to our view that, although markets have recently been focusing on European imbalances, the United States’ fiscal position is far from healthy. As such, our **Base Case Scenario** sees the dollar once again weaken against the euro later in the year, resulting in an annual average rate of 1.38. As inflation begins to accelerate in 2011, we would expect the US monetary authorities to react with higher interest rates, which would likely push the country’s currency into a cyclical recovery. In 2012, we expect the dollar:euro rate to average 1.28. Under **Scenario B** , the dollar is forecast to weaken somewhat further than under the Base Case, as a strong recovery in global markets shakes off much of the sovereign-debt crisis induced

risk aversion. Nevertheless, as economic conditions also improve in North America, providing some support for the greenback, our annual average forecast for 2010 is only modestly higher than under our Base Case, at 1.42. As under this scenario the United States persists with its loose monetary policy next year, further weakness is expected in 2011, leading to a 1.50 average, before a secular recovery commences. In contrast, the swift return of risk aversion under **Scenario C** sees the dollar strengthen through to the end of the forecast period. After an annual average of 1.33 this year, we project dollar:euro rates of 1.29 and 1.23 in 2011 and 2012 respectively. Global Consumption vs Spot Price

In the case of copper, where the overwhelming bulk of activity is essentially unreported, the task becomes ever more difficult. Nevertheless, using what limited data is available and combining that with anecdotal information, that we obtain through field research, conclusions on the direction and relevance of investor activity in copper can be reached. The developments of the first quarter once again confirmed the importance investor activity holds for the copper market. The drop from the upper $7,000s to the trough of just over $6,200/tonne, the strong support at these levels and the remarkable recovery through the $8,000/tonne mark were all in large measure driven by investor activity in the red metal. The graph at the bottom right of this page features weekly investor positions in copper futures listed on the Comex exchange. The figures are calculated using the disaggregated open interest data distributed by the CFTC and includes aggregated net positions for all classes of trading institutions/individuals reported on, excluding “Producer/Merchant/Processor/User”. As can be seen in the chart, the aggregate net long (which is understood to proxy investor positions on the exchange) fell from a peak of more than 850,000 tonnes at the beginning of the year to leve

ls well below 600,000 tonnes in early February, before bouncing back above 700,000 tonnes by early April, broadly in line with the moves in the copper price. It is worth noting that activity in Comex copper futures comprises the smaller part of global investment in copper, with the balance taking place in LME futures, on which disaggregated data on investor and commercial (relating to consumer and producer hedging) positions is not available. Field research over the course of the first quarter revealed an interesting development in investor attitudes towards copper (as well as other industrial commodities). During much of last year commodity investors tended to be “overweight” industrial commodities. This was in part a play on the various stimulus packages that were expected to boost industrial activity as well as more specifically a play on China’s growth. The very low price levels of industrial metals compared to their mid-2008 peaks provided further appeal. Within the sub-sector, copper was often favoured due to its buoyant fundamental outlook, relating to structural constraints to supply growth in the foreseeable future. GFMS do not expect this to be continued in 2010. Industrial metals’ prices - notably that of copper - have already increased considerably; China’s remarkable consumption growth last year suggests that further increases from here onwards are likely to be more limited; although most other economies are also growing, the consensus view is that a full recovery to pre-crisis levels is unlikely to be achieved in the foreseeable future. Although mine capacity growth in the long-term will be constrained, in 2010 a noteworthy - well above-trend - increase is expected. All these issues are well comprehended by the investor community and to our understanding this has led to much of the aforementioned bias towards copper and other industrial commodities evaporating. **~~Rolling 20-day Correlations of Copper Price~~** 1.0

As we discuss in the outlook section of this chapter, the above-discussed short to medium-term outlook for investor activity in copper is key to our view that the next six months will be a period of consolidation for copper prices, under our Base Case. We would expect that any ventures above $8,000/tonne will be capped by profit taking and drops to the low-$6,000s cushioned by “buying-on-dips”. A shift in attitudes to a more one-sided (specifically buying) approach is expected to emerge in the final quarter of the year, as the fundamental market moves into deficit, and we expect this to provide fuel for prices sustainably moving above $8,000/tonne. Looking further ahead, we believe that over the last two years of the forecast period, investors will most probably remain interested in commodities. Moreover, the bullish fundamentals of copper will likely continue to make it a favourite within the sector. Nevertheless, this ongoing reliance of prices on investment demand will continue to make copper

vulnerable to liquidations. As such, our projections for copper prices in 2011 and 2012 see a considerable degree of volatility and regular visits into the $6,000s are expected throughout. 

A key wildcard that could materially affect copper investment demand over the course of the forecast period remains the launch and potential success of the physically backed listed fund, not dissimilar to the precious metals ETFs but closed-ended, that ScotiaMocatta filed for last summer.  Although a recent news article suggested the IPO has now been pulled back, at the time of writing no public announcement has been made on the matter and over the last few months the issuer has filed for and has been granted extensions to submit its final prospectus. 

The precious metals products’ experience suggests that the potential launch and success of a physically backed copper fund could have a dramatic and likely lasting impact on copper prices.  Given the opacity that surrounds the likelihood of the product being launched, GFMS have not included such a development in the assumptions of any of our three scenarios.

###### **1.5 Consumption** 

During the field research in the run-up to our recently launched inaugural _Copper Survey_ , GFMS noted the limited extent to which a recovery in mature markets’ copper consumption has taken place.  The vast majority of our contacts in the industry confirmed that although consistently positive growth was noted, orders in mid to late February 2010 remained far below levels they would have considered normal at pre-crisis times. Coupled with ongoing tightness of liquidity, this has averted any material re-stocking. 

Prompted by the above, we have revised our Base Case projections for 2010 consumption downwards, to a little less than 19 million tonnes for the full year, which represents a 7.6% increase year-on-year.  Reflecting the above-mentioned information, the quarterly breakdown of demand over the course of the year sees the recovery in consumption accelerating in the second half, with the first and second quarter both registering quarter-on-quarter increases below 1%. 

The delayed acceleration of the consumption recovery sees its effects being carried over into the first half of 2011 and, largely as a result of this, global consumption next year grows by 5.4% to reach 20 million tonnes.  Above-trend growth is maintained 

through to 2012, when our base case sees demand falling a little short of 21 million tonnes.  Beyond the three-year forecast period, we would expect a cyclical slow-down to consumption to see growth at levels closer to (potentially below) the 1.7% average recorded over the 1990s. 

###### **1.6 Production** 

Although we are monitoring actively the plethora of planned expansions to mining capacity over the course of the forecast period, GFMS continue to take a conservative view with regard

s to the results these efforts will yield, our analysis clearly influenced by the history of the sector. As such, although our projections for mine and refined production throughout the course of the forecast period see above-trend growth, the rates projected fall short of industry aspirations and, as we discuss in more detail in the following section, are lower than our forecast consumption growth rates. In 2010, as some of the technical and labour-related issues the mining industry was facing last year are reversed and factoring in capacity expansions and growing utilisation rates, mainly in the second half of the year, mine production is expected to increase by 3.9%, providing fuel for a 3.4% increase in refined production. This change in the market’s visible fundamentals is the key explanation for what at first look seems a counterintuitive upward revision to the annual average price for 2010. ### **3.  Copper Consumption** 

###### **3.1 Historical Trends** 

A constant theme of our analysis is the relatively low rate of copper consumption growth during the last decade.  GFMS

estimate the average annual rate over 2000-2009 at just 1.7% per annum, which is one of the lowest rates for all of the base metals.  This partially reflects the high base year of 2000, when copper consumption benefited from the “dot.com” boom.  More importantly, it reflects substitution and miniaturisation issues that have affected copper consumption due to high prices and competition from aluminium and plastics in particular. 

Following the “dot.com” bubble in 2000, and in the aftermath of the 9-11 terrorist attacks in the United States, the mature economies in the Western World suffered a huge loss of confidence.  The authorities’ solution was to flood the market with liquidity and to slash interest rates.  This provided the foundations for one of the strongest bull markets across numerous asset classes, that started in 2003 and ran until 2008. As we have discussed in earlier reports, this boost to liquidity came against a background of tight copper supply and it was this factor rather than strong demand growth that underpinned the bull market in prices. 

This explosion of liquidity fuelled strong growth in consumption spending in mature economies 

(spearheaded by the United States).  In parallel, a number of emerging markets around the world, notably China, experienced rapid industrialisation during the period.  Initially, much of this was focused on servicing mature economies consumption while operating in a lower labour and other operational cost environment, although over the years, as local incomes increased and consumption patterns changed, domestic consumption growth became a key contributor to this trend.  The above saw industrial activity gradually move from mature economies to developing countries and this shift is clearly visible in the regional copper consumption tables. 

In 2000, mature economies consumed 8.935 million tonnes of copper, 59% of world demand.  In the same year, the BRICs consumed 2.652 million tonnes (18%), with other areas consuming 23%.  By 2009, the mature economies consumption had fallen to 5.809 million tonnes, a drop of 35%, but when you consider the global market had grown by 2.521 million tonnes, the mature economies’ relative fall in consumption was significantly larger.  Indeed last year, the mature economies only accounted for 33% of global demand. GFMS notes that the mature economies bore the brunt of the recession in 2009 and project a rebound this year.  However, the downtrend in their share of global consumption looks set to continue.

Asian production increased at an average annual rate of 6.7% over 2000-2009, driven by strong growth in Chinese production. The major concern for Chinese production going forward will be the limitations imposed by concentrate availability, especially given that the ramp up of Jiangxi’s Aynak mine in Afghanistan has been pushed outside of our forecast period.  As a result, the country will become increasingly reliant on the availability of copper scrap.  On this note, new rules regarding the import of scrap metal into China are being implemented over the second quarter.  The rules, aimed at fighting duty evasion, state that scrap will need to be separated by type, while the grade of copper must be documented on customs forms.  This is likely to lead to delays and could discourage imports of scrap into the country.  The tightness in raw material supply is the principal reason for the expected slowdown in growth over the forecast period to an annual average of 4.8% over 2009-12, compared with 13.4% over 2000-09, leading production to a total of 4.830 million tonnes in the final year of our forecast period. 

In **Japan** , following a 7.5% fall last year as a result of the global recession, copper output has been slow to recover in line with strong deflationary pressures and sluggish demand from the construction sector.  We expect this weakness to continue over the forecast period as producers face increased competition for raw materials from Chinese producers.  Similarly, in **India** , although we do see growth of 3.4% in 2012 in line with expansion at Tuticorin, this reliance on imported concentrate is also likely to restrict the country’s production over the period. 

Production in **Kazakhstan** fell 8.4% in 2009, partly as a result of planned maintenance works at Kazakhmys’ Zhezkagan smelter.  Looking forward, we are projecting 

only a marginal rise in production this year in line with Kazakhmys’ announcement that it will keep production largely flat over 2010 as against 2009.  Capacity in the country will however be boosted by the launch of Kazzinc’s 70,000 tonne per year production facility at the Ust-Kamenogorsk metals complex, althoug

h we believe that this, along with restarts at Kazakhmys, will only serve to boost total production in 2011 when we forecast an 8% rise.  Elsewhere, **Indonesia** and **Iran** are also likely to see higher production towards the end of the forecast period. 

###### **Africa** 

Production in Africa grew strongly over the 2000-2009 period, increasing at an average annual rate of 7.7%. However, last year saw diverse performance in the region as the DRC saw strong expansion in line with the start up of Tenke Fungurume, whereas Zambian production suffered in line with the global economic downturn.  Going forward, we expect significant growth in Africa in line with increases in SX-EW production in particular, forecasting average annual growth of 19% over the forecast period. 

The **Democratic Republic of Congo** is expected to build on the 167% increase seen in 2009 production going forward.  As detailed in the mine production section of the report, there are significant SXEW projects coming onstream including the Tenke Fungurume and Luita plants among others, notably Katanga’s operations, which will boost production in the DRC.  Indeed, by 2012, GFMS estimate that production in the DRC will reach 400,000 tonnes, from 170,000 tonnes in 2009, following average growth of 37% over the forecast period.

Production in **Zambia** was affected by lower copper prices last year, falling 2.9% to 405,000 tonnes. 

However, going forward, production will be boosted by a number of projects.  Konkola Copper Mines has recently announced that it has completed expansion of its Nkana refinery to 300,000 tonnes per year.  This is in addition to the start up of the Muliashi plant which is expected to ramp up at an initial 30,000 tonne capacity in 2012. Furthermore, First Minerals has resumed production at its Bwana Mkubwa processing plant.  The plant will use feedstock from the Lonshi mine in the DRC after authorities lifted the ban on copper ore exports, which forced the closure of the plant in the fourth quarter of 2008.  The operation is however only expected to produce around 10,000 tonnes of copper cathode in 2010, significantly lower than the level of around 50,000 tonnes produced at its pea

k in 2006. 

In line with this, GFMS expect Zambian production to increase to 590,000 tonnes in 2012.  Further increases on this total will be reliant on on-going efforts to boost power generation capacity in the region being successful and political risk considerations will also remain an overhanging theme in Africa. 

###### **Oceania** 

GFMS are expecting refined production in **Oceania** to dip by 7.6% this year due to lower output at Olympic Dam.  According to BHP Billiton, Olympic Dam produced just 2,200 tonnes of cathode in the first quarter of the year.  Assuming that Olympic Dam returns to full capacity later this year, we forecast a rise of 15.3% in 2011, with just a 2.0% increase in 2012.  At 500,000 tonnes in 2012, production from the Oceania region will still be down, albeit slightly, on the 2008 figure of 501,500 tonnes. 

###### **Europe** 

GFMS estimate that in 2009 European refined production fell by 4.2%, equivalent to 148,100 tonnes, notably the largest fall since the start of the millennium.  The bulk of the decline comprises of a 65,000 tonne drop in Russian production on the back of cutbacks at two of Russian Copper Company’s (RCC) operations and a combined 83,500 tonne decrease in Scandinavian and Belgian production. 

In terms of our forecast, we believe that reduced output, especially in the countries mentioned above, will be phased back in over the forecast period.  Also, in addition to increases due to RCC’s phasing back of dormant capacity, **Russian** production is expected to benefit from higher utilisation rates, as modestly growing local mine production boosts the availability of concentrate.  In 2011, the commissioning of the Pyshma refinery is also expected to add to the bottom line.  More recently, Russia’s Urals Mining and Metals Co (UMMC) expects this year’s refined copper output to reach 356,918 tonnes, up 8% from 2009. 

Elsewhere, the only major project expected to come on stream is the Las Cruces project in **Spain** .  Las Cruces’ electrowinning operation is due to reach full 72,000 tonnes by 2011, although, as we noted in the mine section, technical problems have limited growth to-date.  In addition, the new UM Pirdop refinery, which opened early in 2008 with an initial capacity of 60,000 tonnes, is expected to reach full capacity by 2010.  This will boost **Bulgarian** production by 5.3% this year to 200,000 tonnes.  All in all, GFMS are forecasting growth in Europe of 3.0% this year, before growth slips in the remaining forecast years.
